hello.title: Hello, C#
hello.summary: Write your first C# program and print text and numbers with `Console.WriteLine`.
hello.lesson.0: A C# program is a list of **statements**. The computer runs them from top to bottom. Your first statement prints a line of text with `Console.WriteLine`.
hello.lesson.2: Text in double quotes, like `"Hello"`, is called a **string**. Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`. If you forget it, the program does not compile.
hello.lesson.4: This one line is already a complete program. Modern C# lets you write statements directly in the file, without any extra structure around them. They are called **top-level statements**. A new project from `dotnet new console` starts exactly like this.
hello.lesson.7: Numbers are written without quotes. C# can calculate with them: `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies and `/` divides.
hello.lesson.9: C# follows the usual math rules: `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`. Parentheses `( )` make C# calculate a part first. A calculation in quotes is only text, so `"2 + 3"` prints as it is.
hello.lesson.11: `Console.Write` prints text without starting a new line afterwards. `Console.WriteLine()` with nothing inside the parentheses only ends the current line.
hello.lesson.13: C# is case-sensitive. `Console.WriteLine` works, but `console.writeline` does not compile.
hello.card.3: `"text"` is a string, `42` is a number
hello-1.explain: C# is case-sensitive, and text must be in double quotes. The method is `Console.WriteLine`.
hello-2.explain: `*` comes before `+`: first `4 * 2` is `8`, then `3 + 8` is `11`.
hello-3.explain: The semicolon is missing. Every statement in C# ends with `;`.
hello-4.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `Hello` and `World` on two separate lines.
hello-4.explain: `WriteLine` ends the line after `Hello`. `Write` would print `HelloWorld` on one line, and `Print` does not exist.
hello-5.explain: `Console.Write` does not start a new line, so `A`, `B` and `C` end up on the same line.
hello-6.explain: The last line has no semicolon. Write `Console.WriteLine("C#");`.
hello-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Hi, Ana!` and then `Bye`.
hello-7.explain: `Console.Write` keeps the first three parts on one line. `WriteLine("!")` ends that line, so `Bye` comes on the next one.
hello-8.prompt: Build a line that prints the result of `6 * 7`.
hello-8.explain: Numbers without quotes are calculated, so the line prints `42`. With quotes, it would print the text `6 * 7`.
hello-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-9.pairs.0: prints x and ends the line
hello-9.pairs.1: prints x without a line break
hello-10.explain: The calculation is inside double quotes, so it is a string. C# prints the text exactly as it is.
hello-11.explain: The parentheses come first: `2 + 3` is `5`, and `5 * 4` is `20`.
hello-12.statement: `Console.Write` starts a new line after the text.
hello-12.explain: Only `Console.WriteLine` ends the line. `Console.Write("A")` followed by `Console.Write("B")` prints `AB`.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in variables and get to know `int`, `double`, `string`, `bool`, `char`, `var` and `const`.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a named box for a value. You create it with a type, a name, `=` and a value. After that, you use the name instead of the value. Variable names usually start with a small letter, like `age` or `firstName`.
variables.lesson.2: You can give a variable a new value later. The old value is then gone. You write the type only once, when you create the variable.
variables.lesson.5: Every variable has a **type** that never changes. `int` holds whole numbers, `double` holds numbers with a decimal point, `string` holds text, `bool` holds `true` or `false`, and `char` holds a single character in single quotes.
variables.lesson.7: `Console.WriteLine` prints a `bool` as `True` or `False` with a capital letter. In code, you always write `true` and `false`.
variables.lesson.8: A variable cannot change its type. `int count = "three";` does not compile, because `"three"` is a `string`, not an `int`.
variables.lesson.10: With `var`, C# works out the type from the value. `var total = 12;` creates an `int`. The type is still fixed: you cannot store text in `total` later.
variables.lesson.12: A `const` is a value that never changes. Giving `MaxPlayers` a new value is an error. Names of constants usually start with a capital letter.
variables.lesson.13: On some computers, a `double` prints with a comma instead of a point, for example `4,5` instead of `4.5`. This depends on the language settings of the system.
variables.card.3: `var x = 5;` lets C# find the type
variables-1.prompt: Match each type with what it holds.
variables-1.pairs.1: a number with a decimal point
variables-2.explain: `x` starts at `5`. Then `5 + 3` is `8`, and `8 * 2` is `16`.
variables-3.prompt: Which line creates a variable that holds a single character?
variables-3.explain: A `char` value is written in single quotes. Double quotes make a `string`, and `x` without quotes is a name, not a value.
variables-4.statement: This code compiles, because a `var` variable can hold any type.
variables-4.explain: `var n = 10;` makes `n` an `int`, and the type never changes. Storing `"ten"` in it is an error.
variables-5.prompt: Fill the gap with the right type.
variables-5.explain: `2.5` has a decimal point, so the type is `double`. An `int` cannot hold `2.5`.
variables-6.explain: `b = a` copies the value `"Hi"` into `b`. Changing `a` later does not change `b`.
variables-7.explain: `Days` is a `const`, so you cannot give it a new value. Remove the line `Days = 8;`.
variables-8.explain: `Console.WriteLine` prints a `bool` with a capital letter: `False`.
variables-9.prompt: Build a line that creates a `string` variable `city` with the value `"Oslo"`.
variables-9.explain: First the type, then the name, then `=` and the value. Text goes in double quotes.
variables-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `32`.
variables-10.explain: A variable must exist before you use it: `height` needs `width`, `area` needs both, and the output comes last.
variables-12.explain: In code you write `true`, but `Console.WriteLine` prints a `bool` with a capital letter.
strings.title: Strings and operators
strings.summary: Join and format text, use string methods like `ToUpper` and `Substring`, and calculate with `%`, `+=` and `++`.
strings.lesson.0: You can join two strings with `+`. This is called **concatenation**. A number joined with a string becomes text too.
strings.lesson.3: A string that starts with `$` can contain values in curly braces, like `$"Hi, {name}!"`. This is called **string interpolation**, and it is often easier to read than `+`. You can also put calculations inside the braces.
strings.lesson.6: `Length` tells you how many characters a string has. `ToUpper()` and `ToLower()` give you the text in capital or small letters. `Substring(start, length)` gives you a part of the string. Positions start at `0`, not at `1`.
strings.lesson.8: `Substring(3)` without a length gives you everything from position `3` to the end. `word[0]` gives you the first character as a `char`. Methods like `ToUpper()` never change the original string. They return a new one.
strings.lesson.10: Besides `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, there is `%`: the remainder of a division. When you divide two `int` values, the result is an `int` too, and the part after the decimal point is cut off. Use a `double` like `7.0` to keep it.
strings.lesson.12: `x += 5` is short for `x = x + 5`. The same works with `-=`, `*=` and `/=`. `x++` adds `1` to `x`, and `x--` subtracts `1`.
strings.lesson.13: `+` with a string and a number joins them as text. `"1" + 2` gives `"12"`, not `3`.
strings-2.explain: `17 / 5` is `3` with a remainder of `2`, and `%` gives the remainder.
strings-3.explain: `"1"` is a string, so `+` joins the text `"1"` and `2` to `"12"`.
strings-4.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `Hi, Lea!`.
strings-4.explain: Only a string that starts with `$` replaces `{name}` with the value of `name`.
strings-5.prompt: Build a line that prints the first 3 characters of `text`.
strings-5.explain: `Substring(0, 3)` starts at position `0` and takes `3` characters.
strings-6.explain: `ToUpper()` returns a new string, but the program does not store it. `s` is still `"cat"`.
strings-7.prompt: The program should print `Rome in 2025`. Which line has the bug?
strings-7.explain: The `$` is missing, so the braces are printed as normal text. Write `$"{city} in {year}"`.
strings-8.explain: `x *= 3` makes `x` `12`, and `x--` subtracts `1`, so it is `11`.
strings-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
strings-9.pairs.4: puts a value into a string
strings-10.prompt: What is the value of `10 / 4` in C#?
strings-10.explain: Both numbers are `int`, so the result is an `int`. The part after the decimal point is cut off.
strings-11.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `HELLO WORLD`.
strings-11.explain: Each line uses the variable from the line before it, so this is the only order that works.
strings-12.explain: Positions start at `0`: `P` is at `0`, `l` at `1` and `a` at `2`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program choose with `if` and `else`, compare values, combine conditions and use switch expressions.
conditions.lesson.0: Programs often need to make a choice. An `if` statement runs a block of code only when its condition is `true`. The block is written in curly braces `{ }`.
conditions.lesson.2: With `else`, you say what happens when the condition is `false`. With `else if`, you check more conditions one after another. C# runs the first block whose condition is `true` and skips the rest.
conditions.lesson.5: A comparison gives a `bool`. The operators are `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<` (less than), `>` (greater than), `<=` (less or equal) and `>=` (greater or equal). You can compare strings with `==` too.
conditions.lesson.7: `=` gives a variable a value, `==` compares two values. `if (a = 5)` does not compile in C#.
conditions.lesson.9: You can combine conditions: `&&` means and (both must be `true`), `||` means or (at least one must be `true`), and `!` means not (it turns `true` into `false` and the other way round).
conditions.lesson.12: A **switch expression** picks one result out of several cases. Each case has the form `value => result`, and the cases are separated by commas. The underscore `_` matches every other value, like a final `else`.
conditions-2.explain: C# runs only the first block whose condition is `true`. `15 > 5` is already `true`, so the other branches are skipped.
conditions-3.explain: `&&` needs both sides to be `true`. `b` is `false`, so the result is `False`.
conditions-4.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `Equal`.
conditions-4.explain: `==` compares two values. A single `=` assigns a value and does not compile inside `if`.
conditions-5.explain: `else` never has a condition. Write only `else`, or use `else if (age < 18)`.
conditions-6.prompt: Match the operator with its meaning.
conditions-6.pairs.1: at least one must be true
conditions-6.pairs.4: any other value in a switch
conditions-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Even`.
conditions-8.explain: Each variable needs the one before it. In the switch expression, `_` must be the last case, because it matches every value.
conditions-9.prompt: Build the line that checks that `age` is at least `18` and `member` is `true`.
conditions-9.explain: `>=` means greater or equal, and `&&` needs both conditions to be `true`.
conditions-10.explain: `||` is `true` when at least one side is `true`. `&&` means and, `!` means not.
conditions-11.statement: In a switch expression, `_` matches every value that no other case matched.
conditions-11.explain: `_` is the discard pattern. It works like a final `else`.
conditions-12.explain: `a > b` is `false`, so `!(a > b)` is `true`. But `b != 8` is `false`, and `true && false` is `False`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with `for`, `while` and `foreach`, and control a loop with `break` and `continue`.
loops.lesson.0: A **loop** repeats code. The `for` loop is the classic way to count. It has three parts in parentheses, separated by semicolons: a start, a condition and a step.
loops.lesson.2: `int i = 1` runs once at the start. Before each round, C# checks `i <= 3`. After each round, `i++` adds `1` to `i`. As soon as the condition is `false`, the loop ends. A loop is also useful to add up numbers.
loops.lesson.5: A `while` loop repeats its block as long as the condition is `true`. Use it when you do not know in advance how many rounds you need. Make sure the condition becomes `false` at some point, or the loop never ends.
loops.lesson.8: A `foreach` loop goes through every item of a collection, one after another. A string is a collection of characters, so you can loop over it. You meet more collections in a later world.
loops.lesson.11: `break` ends the whole loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next round.
loops.lesson.13: To count down, start high and use `i--`. The loop `for (int i = 3; i > 0; i--)` counts `3`, `2`, `1`.
loops.card.3: `break` ends the loop, `continue` skips one round
loops-1.explain: `i` starts at `0` and the loop runs while `i < 4`, so it prints `0`, `1`, `2` and `3` on one line.
loops-2.explain: `i` takes the values `2`, `4` and `6`. Their sum is `12`.
loops-3.prompt: How many times does this loop print `Hi`?
loops-3.explain: `i` takes the values `1`, `2`, `3` and `4`. When `i` is `5`, `i < 5` is `false` and the loop ends.
loops-4.prompt: Fill the gap so the loop prints `5`, `4`, `3`, `2`, `1`.
loops-4.explain: `i--` subtracts `1` after each round. `i - 1` calculates a value but does not change `i`, and `i -= 2` skips numbers.
loops-5.statement: A `while` loop whose condition is `false` at the start never runs its block.
loops-5.explain: C# checks the condition before every round, including the first one.
loops-6.prompt: The program should print `1`, `2` and `3`. Which line has the bug?
loops-6.explain: With `i < 3`, the loop stops before `3` is printed. Write `while (i <= 3)`.
loops-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `14`.
loops-7.explain: `total` must exist before the loop. In each round, the loop calculates `square` and adds it: `1 + 4 + 9` is `14`. The result is printed once, after the loop.
loops-8.prompt: Build a loop header that goes through every character `c` of `word`.
loops-8.explain: A `foreach` loop has the form `foreach (type name in collection)`.
loops-9.prompt: Match the keyword with its meaning.
loops-9.pairs.0: counts with a start, a condition and a step
loops-9.pairs.1: repeats as long as a condition is true
loops-10.explain: When `i` is `3`, `break` ends the loop before `3` is printed.
loops-11.explain: The loop looks at every character of `"banana"`, and three of them are `'a'`.
loops-12.explain: For odd numbers, `i % 2 == 1` is `true` and `continue` skips the output. Only `2` and `4` are printed.
methods.title: Methods
methods.summary: Write your own methods with parameters, return values and optional parameters, and call them as often as you need.
methods.lesson.0: A **method** is a named block of code that you can run as often as you want. You already use methods like `Console.WriteLine`. Now you write your own.
methods.lesson.2: `void` means that the method gives nothing back. The name is followed by parentheses, and method names in C# start with a capital letter. To run a method, you **call** it: write its name with parentheses.
methods.lesson.3: **Parameters** are inputs of a method. Each parameter has a type and a name. When you call the method, you pass a value for each parameter, called an **argument**. Inside the method, the parameter is a new variable with a copy of that value.
methods.lesson.6: A method can calculate a value and give it back with `return`. Instead of `void`, you write the type of the result before the name. `return` also ends the method at once.
methods.lesson.8: If a method only returns one expression, you can use the short form with `=>`. The method `IsEven` below returns a `bool`.
methods.lesson.11: A parameter with a default value is **optional**. If you leave out the argument, C# uses the default. You can also write the name of a parameter in the call, like `count: 2`. Then the order of the arguments does not matter.
methods.lesson.13: Here the methods live directly in the program file, next to the top-level statements. Methods inside a class, which you meet in the last world, work the same way.
methods.card.1: `int Add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`
methods.card.3: `void Hi(string name = "you")` has an optional parameter
methods-1.explain: The inner call runs first: `Add(3, 4)` is `7`, and `Add(2, 7)` is `9`.
methods-2.prompt: What does `void` before a method name mean?
methods-2.explain: `void` stands where the type of the result would be. It says that the method gives nothing back.
methods-3.prompt: Fill the gap so the method gives back the doubled value.
methods-3.explain: `return` gives the value back to the caller, so `Twice(5)` is `10`.
methods-4.explain: `Shout` has a parameter, so the call needs an argument, for example `Shout("hey")`.
methods-5.statement: A method with the return type `int` must give back a value with `return`.
methods-5.explain: The type before the name promises a result. Without `return`, the method does not compile.
methods-6.explain: The call passes `"#"`, so it replaces the default value `"*"`.
methods-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the method returns the price of all items plus a fee of `2`.
methods-7.explain: The method starts with its header and `{`. Each variable needs the one before it, and `return` gives back the final result.
methods-8.prompt: Build a short method `Next` that returns its argument plus one.
methods-8.explain: The short form is the type of the result, the name with the parameters, `=>` and the expression.
methods-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
methods-9.pairs.1: gives x back and ends the method
methods-9.pairs.2: a parameter with a default value
methods-9.pairs.4: calls a method with an argument
methods-10.explain: `Calc(3)` uses the default `b = 10` and gives `30`. `Calc(2, 2)` gives `4`. Together that is `34`.
methods-11.explain: `-5 < 0` is `true`, so the first `return` ends the method with `"negative"`.
methods-12.explain: The method gets a copy of the value of `n`. Changing `x` inside the method does not change `n`, so the program prints `5`.
collections.title: Arrays and lists
collections.summary: Store many values in arrays, lists and dictionaries, and go through them with `foreach`.
collections.lesson.1: An **array** stores several values of the same type in one variable. You write the type with square brackets, like `int[]`, and the values in `[ ]`. Each value has a position, the **index**, which starts at `0`.
collections.lesson.3: The last index is `Length - 1`. Reading `scores[3]` from an array with three items stops the program with an `IndexOutOfRangeException`.
collections.lesson.5: An array has a fixed size. A `List<T>` can grow and shrink. `T` stands for the type of the items, so `List<string>` is a list of strings. `Add` adds an item at the end, `Remove` deletes one, and `Count` tells you how many items there are.
collections.lesson.7: `foreach` goes through all items of an array or a list. To print all items on one line, use `string.Join` with a separator.
collections.lesson.9: `Console.WriteLine(numbers)` does not print the items, only the name of the type. Use `string.Join` or a loop instead.
collections.lesson.11: A `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` stores pairs of a **key** and a **value**. You look up a value by its key, like a word in a dictionary. Each key exists only once.
collections.lesson.13: `new Dictionary<string, int>()` creates an empty dictionary with `string` keys and `int` values. Assigning to `ages["Ana"]` again replaces the old value. Reading a key that does not exist stops the program, so check it with `ContainsKey` first.
collections-1.explain: The index starts at `0`: `a[0]` is `4`, `a[1]` is `7` and `a[2]` is `1`.
collections-2.explain: The list starts with two names, gets two more and loses one: `2 + 2 - 1` is `3`.
collections-3.prompt: Which index does the first item of an array have?
collections-3.explain: In C#, counting positions starts at `0`. The second item has the index `1`.
collections-4.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `3`.
collections-4.explain: A list tells you its number of items with `Count`. `Length` is for arrays and strings.
collections-5.explain: The array has three items, so the last index is `2`. Write `colors[2]`.
collections-6.statement: An array can grow: you can call `Add` on an `int[]`.
collections-6.explain: An array has a fixed size and no `Add` method. Use a `List<int>` if you need to add items.
collections-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `7`.
collections-7.explain: First create the dictionary, then store `10` for the key `"pens"`. Only then can you subtract `3` and print the result.
collections-8.prompt: Build a line that creates a `List<string>` named `drinks` with `"tea"` and `"milk"`.
collections-8.explain: The type comes first, then the name, `=` and the items in square brackets.
collections-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
collections-9.pairs.1: a list of texts that can grow
collections-9.pairs.2: pairs of a key and a value
collections-9.pairs.3: number of items in a list
collections-9.pairs.4: number of items in an array
collections-10.explain: The second assignment to `"tea"` replaces `3` with `4`. There are still only two keys, so the result is `4 + 2`.
collections-11.explain: The loop adds the squares `4`, `16` and `36`, which is `56`.
collections-12.explain: `Add(3)` adds `3` at the end, and `nums[0] = 9` replaces the first item. `string.Join` puts `-` between the items.
classes.title: Classes and objects
classes.summary: Define your own types with classes, properties, constructors and methods, and store data with records.
classes.lesson.0: A **class** is a blueprint for your own type. It bundles data and the methods that work with that data. An **object** is one concrete thing that you build from a class with `new`.
classes.lesson.2: `Name` and `Age` are **properties**: values that every object of the class has. `{ get; set; }` means you can read and change them, and `public` means code outside the class can use them. `= ""` gives `Name` an empty text as start value. In a program with top-level statements, classes go at the end of the file.
classes.lesson.4: A **constructor** runs when you create an object with `new`. It has the same name as the class and no return type. Use it to give the properties their start values.
classes.lesson.6: A property with only `get` can be set in the constructor, but not changed later. This protects the data of an object from mistakes.
classes.lesson.8: A class can have methods that use the properties of the object. Each object keeps its own values, so the same method changes only the object you call it on. `private set` means that only code inside the class can change `Value`.
classes.lesson.11: A **record** is a short way to define a type that mainly holds data. One line creates the properties and the constructor. Records also print their values in a readable way, and two records with the same values are equal.
classes.lesson.13: Two objects of a normal class are only equal with `==` if they are the very same object. Use a record when you want to compare the values.
classes.card.0: `class Dog { public string Name { get; set; } = ""; }`
classes.card.1: `var d = new Dog();` creates an object
classes.card.2: `public Dog(string name) { Name = name; }` is a constructor
classes.card.3: `record Point(int X, int Y);` is a data type
classes.card.4: Classes go after the top-level statements
classes-1.explain: `Lives` is set to `9`, and `-= 2` makes it `7`.
classes-2.prompt: Which expression creates a new object of the class `Car`?
classes-2.explain: You create objects with the keyword `new`, followed by the class name and parentheses.
classes-3.prompt: Fill the gap so the constructor stores the name.
classes-3.explain: The property `Name` gets the value of the parameter `name`. `name = name` would only assign the parameter to itself.
classes-4.statement: A constructor has the same name as its class and no return type.
classes-4.explain: That is how C# recognizes a constructor. It runs every time you create an object with `new`.
classes-5.explain: `Area` returns a number, so its return type must be `int`, not `void`. Write `public int Area()`.
classes-6.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Hi, Ana`.
classes-6.explain: The top-level statements come first and the class goes at the end. Create the object before you set or read `Name`.
classes-7.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
classes-7.pairs.2: a property you can read and change
classes-7.pairs.3: a data type that compares values
classes-8.explain: Records compare their values. Both records have the name `"pen"`, so `a == b` is `True`.
classes-9.prompt: Build the line that defines a record `Person` with a `Name` and an `Age`.
classes-9.explain: A record lists its properties with their types in parentheses after the name.
classes-10.explain: Each call of `Sell` adds to `Sold` of the same object: `3 + 4` is `7`.
classes-11.explain: `Box` is a normal class. `a` and `b` are two different objects, so `a == b` is `False`.
